title: When Your Top Feature Makes Predictions Worse
hook: A feature can top your model's importance ranking and still hurt accuracy. The only way to be sure it helps: delete it, retrain, and compare on held-out data.
key_points: Feature importance measures how much a model leaned on a feature, not whether it improves generalization.
A practitioner's fancy target-encoded feature ranked #1 by a wide margin across seeds.
A strict hold-out ablation (remove it, retrain) reversed the verdict — error got worse with it in.
Target/Bayesian encoders can leak label information, inflating in-sample importance.
Trust ablations on a held-out set over the model's built-in importance scores.
content_html: A team forecasting secondary-market watch prices with LightGBM built a clever variant-conditioned Bayesian target encoder, and the model adored it: at the 90th-percentile quantile it ranked as the #1 feature by a wide margin, consistently across random seeds. By the usual "what matters most?" readout, it was the star of the model.
extra_html: Then they ran a disciplined ablation — drop the feature, retrain, and measure error on a held-out set across multiple seeds and product variants. The result inverted: the model was actually worse with the prized feature than without it. The likely culprit is a classic gradient-boosting trap: target-based encoders can leak information about the label into the training features, so the model leans on them heavily (high importance) without genuinely generalizing. The lesson is durable — feature importance describes what a model used, not what helps. When it matters, settle it with an ablation on data the model never saw. Reported by the practitioner on r/MachineLearning.

related.title: Cross-Validation
related.hook: One lucky or unlucky split can flatter or sink your model. Rotate the holdout and average — that's cross-validation.

related.title: Train / Validation / Test Splits
related.hook: If you tune and grade on the same data, you'll fool yourself. Keep a test set you never touch until the very end.

related.title: The Bias–Variance Tradeoff
related.hook: Too simple and your model misses the pattern; too flexible and it chases noise. Generalization lives between the two.

flashcards.prompt: How can a feature rank #1 in importance yet make a model worse?
flashcards.back_html: Importance measures how heavily the model relied on the feature during training, not whether it helps on new data. Leakage (e.g. from target encoding) can inflate that reliance while hurting generalization.

flashcards.prompt: What most reliably tells you whether a feature actually helps?

choices.text: Remove it, retrain, and compare error on a held-out set (ablation)
Its rank in the model's built-in feature-importance scores
How strongly it correlates with the other features

flashcards.explanation_html: Built-in importance reflects in-sample reliance and can be fooled by leakage. A hold-out ablation measures the feature's real effect on generalization — here it flipped the verdict.
